outcome: No accepted or expert-vetted result has changed the status of the Ulam density problem since 26 January 2024; it remains open. A long-running, unpublished, unreviewed arXiv preprint by Theophilus Agama claiming zero density has been repeatedly revised (including in the window, up to v12 on 2026-03-10) but shows no sign of expert acceptance, and mainstream researchers working on Ulam sequences in 2024-2025 (e.g. Clément & Steinerberger) continue to treat the density question as open and do not cite or build on Agama's claim.
summary: The problem asks whether the Ulam numbers (1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11, 13, ...) have positive natural density; empirically they appear to have density around 0.07398, but no proof of positive density (or of zero density) has been accepted by the mathematical community. The triage record correctly flagged a preprint by Theophilus Agama, 'Ulam numbers have zero density' (arXiv:2007.02697), which directly addresses this exact question and has an active revision history extending into the window (v1 in July 2020, up through v12 on 2026-03-10 — well inside the 26 Jan 2024 to present window). I read the abstract/PDF (via WebFetch) and searched extensively for any expert digestion, MathOverflow discussion, journal acceptance, or citation of this claim by other researchers. I found none. The paper is also mirrored on vixra.org, a repository generally used for work that has not passed, or was not submitted to, mainstream peer review or arXiv endorsement scrutiny — a signal consistent with a claim that has not been vetted. Most importantly, the claimed conclusion (zero density) runs directly counter to strong numerical evidence accumulated over decades (density ≈0.07398, and more recent 2024-2025 work by Clément and Steinerberger on growth bounds and periodic gap structure that presumes/supports a persistent, non-vanishing density of Ulam numbers). Active 2024-2025 research on Ulam sequences and Ulam words (Clément & Steinerberger, Comptes Rendus Math 2025; a 2024 INTEGERS paper on Ulam words) neither cites nor engages with Agama's claim, which is the behavior expected if the mathematical community does not regard it as an established or even seriously considered resolution. Since repeated revision of an unrefereed, uncited preprint that contradicts strong numerical evidence does not meet the bar for `claimed` (which requires the claim itself to have been taken up as a live claim, e.g. announced and discussed) as much as it reflects one author's persistent, apparently unresolved and unengaged assertion, I classify this as `open` with `no_change_found` true, rather than `claimed`. No AI system appears anywhere in the record of work on this problem in the window.
competing_reading: One could argue for `claimed` status on the grounds that Agama's preprint is a standing, undisclaimed proof claim that overlaps the window (the v12 revision in March 2026 is a fresh, in-window restatement of the claim), and that its mere existence as an unretracted proof attempt on arXiv is itself an 'event' worth recording under `claimed`, with `resolution_direction` refuted (since it claims zero density against the historically conjectured/expected positive density). Under this reading, the persistence of the preprint through 12 versions without withdrawal, and its continued availability, could be treated as a `claimed` resolution that experts simply haven't gotten around to formally rejecting. I did not adopt this reading because `claimed` in this schema is meant for claims that have entered live consideration by the field (an announcement drawing discussion, a preprint drawing engagement) — and I found zero evidence of any expert (on MathOverflow, in a citing paper, in a blog, or elsewhere) treating this specific claim as live, discussing it, or refuting it. A years-long, self-revised, uncited, un-discussed preprint contradicting strong numerical evidence looks more like an unengaged assertion than a claim under active consideration.
what_would_settle_it: Any of: (a) a citation of or response to Agama's arXiv:2007.02697 by another mathematician (acceptance, refutation, or even serious engagement) in a paper, blog, or forum; (b) journal acceptance or rejection of the paper; (c) a MathOverflow or similar expert discussion thread addressing the specific claim; (d) a statement on the Wikipedia Ulam number article or Ulam sequence OEIS page referencing this claim; (e) any statement in a 2024-2026 Ulam-sequence paper (e.g. by Steinerberger's group) explicitly addressing why Agama's claimed zero-density proof is or is not compelling.
